KEY MESSAGE 1...Potential fog development this morning and 
again overnight tonight, but otherwise, generally tranquil 
weather prevails through the middle of the week.

High pressure will remain in place within the vicinity of our 
area through the middle of the week. Dry weather is expected to 
continue through Wednesday amid warming temperatures each day.

Scattered to broken high cloud cover will persist through the 
middle of the week despite surface high pressure. Temperatures 
are expected to increase back to above normal values, warming 
each day through Wednesday. High temperatures look to be in the 
upper 60s to low 70s Tuesday, and in the low to mid 70s 
Wednesday. Overnights will becoming increasingly milder (no 
frost/freeze potential). Dry weather is expected to persist 
through Wednesday.

There is potential for areas of fog development early this
morning and again overnight tonight into early Wednesday morning.
Dewpoints will also be on the rise each day. Given mostly clear
skies, light winds, and long nights, we anticipate some fog 
development across the area during the overnight periods. The 
latest hi-res guidance continues to suggest the best chance for
fog development will be along and southeast of the I-95 
corridor and across the coastal plain. Confidence remains low on
any dense fog. Where fog does develop, it will likely be slow 
to mix out after sunrise Tuesday and Wednesday mornings. Light 
southerly flow will promote dewpoint advection and the solar 
insolation is relatively weak until closer to midday, which will
limit mixing earlier in the morning.


KEY MESSAGE 2...The next chance for rain returns late this week and 
into the weekend.

The ridging that has be in place across the area for the past 
several days will finally begin to break down by Wednesday night 
into Thursday as a potent upper trough over central CONUS cuts off 
and lifts northeastward into portions of the Great Lakes and 
southern Canada by the end of the week. As this occurs, broad 
troughing is expected to take shape across the eastern CONUS as a 
few lobes of upper level energy will pivot through the region 
Thursday and over the weekend. At the surface, low pressure over the 
Midwest is forecast to track northeast into Canada as it weakens 
into Thursday with a trailing cold front back to the southwest.
Latest guidance shows this frontal boundary washing out and
stalling across the region Thursday night. General QPF guidance
shows around 0.25 to 0.35 inches through daybreak Friday. After
this time, there is still considerable uncertainty as to how 
this system will evolve to impact our local area.

Heading into Friday, while uncertainty remains, the latest
guidance shows a polar trough phasing with a lobe of upper level
energy, resulting in a rather poignant troughing patter across
the eastern US. Guidance varies on the exact evolution of this
trough through Friday, but several models show it digging before
ultimately becoming a cut-off low across the Mid Atlantic or
Northeastern states by Friday night. In the process, a surface
low may form along the previously stalled boundary, beginning
across VA/NC and trekking along the front into coastal New
England. PWAT values look to creep up into the 1.50-1.75" range,
which would push into the climatological maximum for this time
of year. QPF forecasts this far out are also pointing out the
potential for a corridor of heavy rainfall of a few inches or
more, though the exact placement of where the heaviest rain will
occur remains highly uncertain at this time. 

Heading into this weekend, surface high pressure attempts to
build in from the west, but will struggle to gain full control
with broad upper level troughing and a cut-off low pattern
overhead. Any upper level pattern like this will be highly
dependent on how these cut-off lows and their lobes of shortwave
energy evolve, a set-up which always bring more uncertainty 
than usual to the forecast. The takeaway message here is that
the weekend may not be fully dry and could remain somewhat
unsettled.
